nodes.label: _intent_label() score-to-level mapping
nodes.rationale: Jev returns a continuous score plus a legend; the score is rounded and clamped to the nearest level, and the legend mapping is preferred over the raw index so a future reordering on the vendor's side cannot silently shift the mapping.

nodes.label: JevRunner.run()
nodes.rationale: Three attempts with connection teardown and backoff, because a reused keep-alive socket can drop; emits the same prediction/confidence/latency/cost record shape as ClaudeRunner so score.py needs no per-runner branches.

nodes.label: COMPETITOR_CLARIFICATION (v2 prompt delta)
nodes.rationale: Round 1 said 'a direct competitor' and never said who that is, so Haiku threw out Workday, Atlassian, ServiceNow and Oracle for also selling software. That is a fair complaint about the prompt, not only the model, so round 2 names Clay, Apollo, ZoomInfo, Outreach and Salesloft and changes nothing else. Both models get it.

nodes.label: noul probability with a 0.5 decision threshold
nodes.norm_label: noul probability with a 0.5 decision threshold
nodes.rationale: A noul answer is a probability, not a boolean: 0.5 is applied as the decision threshold for the prediction while the raw probability is kept separately so calibration (Brier, ECE) can be scored without re-running the benchmark.

nodes.label: Business error metric: funded buyers binned
nodes.norm_label: business error metric: funded buyers binned
nodes.rationale: Counts leads whose true route is ae_now but whose predicted route is reject. Accuracy treats every mistake the same; this one does not, because binning a funded buyer costs revenue. Haiku did it to 7 of 16, Sonnet to 1, Jev to 0.

nodes.label: Business error metric: disqualified leads leaked
nodes.norm_label: business error metric: disqualified leads leaked
nodes.rationale: Counts leads labelled disqualify that the model let through. Handing a competitor a demo costs something worse than revenue; this is where Jev's 2-of-12 competitor blind spot shows up against the 90% headline.

nodes.label: Route accuracy (the end-to-end workflow metric)
nodes.rationale: How often the whole workflow put the lead in the right queue, which is the only number a GTM team feels. Computed by pushing both the prediction and the label through the same spec.route().

nodes.label: v1 / v2 prompt variants
nodes.rationale: v1 is the prompt as originally written; v2 is v1 plus one sentence naming the competitor set on the disqualify question and nothing else, so the round-to-round delta is attributable to exactly that sentence. Unknown variant strings raise rather than silently falling back to v1.

nodes.label: Result record: jev
nodes.rationale: v1: 90.0% route accuracy, 366ms p50, $0.042 per 1,000, Brier 0.041/0.041, 0 of 16 funded buyers binned, 2 of 12 disqualified leaked. v2 holds route accuracy at exactly 90.0% with icp_fit up to 96.7%.

nodes.label: Routing belongs in code, not a model
nodes.norm_label: routing belongs in code, not a model
nodes.rationale: Five branches that are free, instant, testable and cannot drift. Spending a model call on a branch buys nothing and adds a failure mode you paid for. What the models are for is the four genuinely fuzzy judgments underneath.

nodes.label: Jev's competitor blind spot (L009 Clay, L010 Apollo.io)
nodes.norm_label: jev's competitor blind spot (l009 clay, l010 apollo.io)
nodes.rationale: Jev's two disqualify misses were a RevOps manager at Clay and a PM at Apollo.io, waved through at 0.06 and 0.18. Naming the competitor set in round 2 flipped both for Sonnet (0.95 and 0.97) but never moved Jev over the line: Jev is better at applying a rubric you describe, Claude is better at using a fact you just told it. The real fix is a domain blocklist in code, not a model.

nodes.label: Jev's half-level intent optimism bias
nodes.rationale: Intent is Jev's worst number at 75% against Sonnet's 82%. Of 15 errors, 14 are off by exactly one level and every one runs the same direction: it reads leads as keener than they are. A systematic bias of about half a level is fixable with a threshold rather than a different model.

nodes.label: Recommended production architecture
nodes.rationale: Domain blocklist first because it is the one step with a right answer needing no model; Jev for the four fuzzy judgments; routing in code because it is five branches that are free, instant, untestable-by-drift and unit testable; Sonnet only on qualified leads. Jev's Brier of 0.041 against Sonnet's 0.130 means the probability is usable for an auto-approve band above 0.9 and a human-review band at 0.4-0.6. Send intent to human review until recalibrated.

nodes.label: _coerce() near-miss label normaliser
nodes.rationale: Accepts a near-miss label (case, hyphen, prefix) rather than scoring a formatting slip as a wrong answer.

nodes.label: ClaudeRunner._invoke() CLI subprocess call
nodes.rationale: Shells out to the claude CLI in print mode because no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY was on the machine, replacing the CLI system prompt, disallowing tools, setting effort low, and exporting MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0 to switch extended thinking off.

nodes.label: _parse_json() fence-tolerant parser
nodes.rationale: Claude was told to return bare JSON, but a markdown fence is tolerated anyway so a formatting slip is not scored as a wrong judgment.

nodes.label: ClaudeRunner.calibrate() CLI overhead measurement
nodes.rationale: Sends an empty system prompt and a one-character user message five times and takes the median, summing input_tokens plus both cache buckets because Sonnet's CLI caches the prompt and input_tokens alone reads 2. Without the sum the overhead measures as zero and Claude is billed for scaffolding it did not write.

nodes.label: PRICING and cache multipliers
nodes.rationale: Published list prices for Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5, with cache writes at 1.25x and reads at 0.1x of the base input rate, because the CLI's system-prompt caching is a real saving a production deployment would also get.

nodes.label: ClaudeRunner.run()
nodes.rationale: Reports duration_api_ms rather than wall clock so CLI process startup is excluded, and keeps the raw probabilities in a separate `confidence` block so calibration can be scored later without re-running.

nodes.label: JevRunner.measure_connect_cost() TLS handshake floor
nodes.rationale: Median wall time of a cold TCP+TLS handshake, reported alongside the results so the network floor is visible instead of being quietly folded into the model's latency number.

nodes.label: ClaudeSplitRunner.run()
nodes.rationale: Sums latency, tokens and cost across the four calls and reports requests=4, so the ablation's real overhead is visible in the same table as the single-call runs.

nodes.label: House rule: fix the unfair thing even when it helps the other side
nodes.norm_label: house rule: fix the unfair thing even when it helps the other side
nodes.rationale: The first version of the table was wrong in Claude's disfavour (thinking on by default, cache reads billed at list price). A benchmark that only corrects in one direction is not worth publishing.

nodes.label: House rules for the benchmarks
nodes.rationale: Six self-imposed rules written as a reaction to vendor benchmarks; they are the reason the numbers here are lower than the ones in launch posts.

nodes.label: House rule: measure the network, not just the model
nodes.norm_label: house rule: measure the network, not just the model
nodes.rationale: Jev's first call looked like 970ms, but ~600ms was the TLS handshake and ~290ms was round trip time, leaving roughly 80ms of actual inference. Every latency number states which is which rather than folding the network floor into the model's number.

nodes.label: House rule: publish the failures
nodes.rationale: Every raw response is committed to results/raw/, including the wrong ones, so a reader who distrusts a number can check it.

nodes.label: House rule: both sides get the same words
nodes.norm_label: house rule: both sides get the same words
nodes.rationale: Prompts are generated from one shared spec file. Jev gets the criteria as typed questions, Claude gets the same strings rendered as text, so neither sees wording the other did not get and accuracy differences are attributable to the model.

nodes.label: Fairness correction: CLI token-overhead calibration
nodes.rationale: Because of prompt caching, the calibration probe read the wrong field and measured Sonnet's CLI scaffolding as 2 tokens instead of 2,214, so Claude was billed for a prompt it did not write. Summing all three token buckets fixed it and dropped Sonnet's cost per thousand from $7.71 to $3.01.

nodes.label: Fairness correction: prompt-cache-aware pricing
nodes.rationale: Sonnet's CLI caches the system prompt so its real tokens land in cache_creation and cache_read, not input_tokens. Cache reads were being charged at full input price; writes bill at 1.25x and reads at 0.1x, and Claude gets credit for that saving because a production deployment would get it too.

nodes.label: Fairness correction: extended thinking disabled
nodes.rationale: The Claude CLI enables extended thinking by default; Haiku spent ~1,800 thinking tokens and 22 seconds per lead deciding whether a resume was a resume. MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0 took the same call to 2.6 seconds. Nobody would ship lead triage with thinking on, so benchmarking it that way would have been dishonest by a factor of 23.

nodes.label: QUESTIONS (shared typed question definitions)
nodes.rationale: Single source of truth: Jev receives these dicts as typed questions and claude_runner renders the same strings as prose, so a rubric change lands on both sides at once. That is the only way the accuracy numbers mean anything.

nodes.label: Typed judgment: disqualify (noul / probability)
nodes.rationale: Asked as a noul (probability) question so the answer carries calibration, not just a boolean. Explicitly tells the model not to disqualify a real buyer for a personal email address, a short message, or a small company.

nodes.label: Typed judgment: icp_fit (noul / probability)
nodes.rationale: Three conjunctive conditions (B2B, 50+ employees, revenue/marketing/ops/data/exec role), judged on company and role rather than email domain, and deliberately kept independent of disqualify.

nodes.label: Typed judgment: intent (score over an ordered ladder)
nodes.norm_label: typed judgment: intent (score over an ordered ladder)
nodes.rationale: Modelled as a continuous score over four ordered levels rather than a choice, judging urgency and specificity of the message and not company quality. This is the one judgment where Jev loses to both Claude models.

nodes.label: Typed judgment: segment (choice)
nodes.rationale: A choice question over enterprise / mid_market / smb driven by headcount, with inference from the company name only when headcount is missing. Every runner scores 95-100% on it, which is what makes it useful as a floor.

nodes.label: Six-step inbound lead triage workflow
nodes.rationale: Steps 1-4 (disqualify, icp_fit, segment, intent) are judgments and go to a model; step 5 (routing) is a rule and runs in code for every runner; step 6 (writing the email) is prose and goes to Claude because Jev structurally cannot produce it. Splitting the workflow this way is what makes the cost comparison meaningful.

nodes.label: Rubric: disqualify rule
nodes.rationale: True for job applicants, students or academics wanting free access, vendors and agencies, competitor employees, and spam. A short message or a gmail address is not a disqualification. Competitors are judged by employer, not by what they wrote, because that is how they present in a real inbox.

nodes.label: Rubric: icp_fit rule
nodes.rationale: True when the company sells to businesses, has 50+ headcount, and the role touches revenue, marketing, ops, data or is executive. Judge the company not the email domain (L016 is a real Cisco buyer on gmail); judge the role not the seniority (L044 is a Facilities Coordinator at Salesforce and is not a fit).

nodes.label: Rubric: intent rule
nodes.rationale: Four ordered levels (none, researching, evaluating, ready_to_buy) judged on the message and not the company. Support tickets from large existing customers are none no matter the account size (L046, L048), while an expansion order is ready_to_buy (L047) because expansion is a purchase.

nodes.label: Rubric: five-branch routing rule
nodes.rationale: Routing is a rule so it runs as one: the same function runs over the answer key and over each model's output, and no model is ever asked to route. This is the part people usually hand to a model and the part a model should never touch.

nodes.label: Rubric: segment rule
nodes.rationale: Straight from headcount: 1000+ enterprise, 200-999 mid_market, under 200 smb. Included deliberately as a floor: a model that gets this wrong has a reading problem, not a judgment problem.

nodes.label: Jev Playground (weekly benchmark repo)
nodes.rationale: A weekly series that builds something real with Jev and publishes the measurements, on the premise that the useful question is not 'is Jev better than Claude' but which steps of a workflow are decisions and which are writing.

nodes.label: Week 01: inbound lead triage and routing
nodes.norm_label: week 01: inbound lead triage and routing

nodes.label: Correlated-error hypothesis (Haiku conflates disqualify and icp_fit)
nodes.norm_label: correlated-error hypothesis (haiku conflates disqualify and icp_fit)
nodes.rationale: All 29 of Haiku's icp_fit errors ran the same direction and lined up with 27 over-disqualifications: it decided 'bad lead' once and wrote that answer into both fields. That could be an artifact of the single-JSON format rather than the model, so the ablation removes the format to test it.

nodes.label: Judgment independence (icp_fit judged separately from disqualify)
nodes.norm_label: judgment independence (icp_fit judged separately from disqualify)
nodes.rationale: A RevOps manager at a competitor is a fit on company and role and still gets rejected, because the routing rule checks disqualification first. Keeping the two questions separate stops one judgment from quietly absorbing another and makes a model that confuses them visible in the numbers.

nodes.label: USD_PER_INPUT_TOKEN ($42 per billion, input only)
nodes.rationale: Output tokens are not billed at all, because the output is a label and a number rather than prose.

nodes.label: Jev typed decision model
nodes.rationale: You send state plus typed questions and get back a choice, a score, or a probability with a confidence. It cannot write prose, and that is the point: output is a label and a number, so input bills at $42 per billion tokens and output is free.

nodes.label: LEADS (60 hand-labelled lead records)
nodes.rationale: Each tuple carries the lead fields plus the four hand-written labels. No model produced any label; the route is deliberately not stored but computed by spec.route() so the answer key and the models pass through the same function.

nodes.label: 60-lead label distribution
nodes.rationale: 12 disqualify / 48 not; 44 icp_fit / 16 not; 24 enterprise, 19 mid_market, 17 smb; intent 13/14/20/13; routes 16 ae_now, 19 nurture, 10 sdr_sequence, 12 reject, 3 self_serve. self_serve has only 3 cases so that confusion-matrix row is directional only.

nodes.label: Lead triage rubric and answer key
nodes.norm_label: lead triage rubric and answer key
nodes.rationale: Published so a reader can disagree with the labelling rules; the fix for a mislabelled lead is a pull request against build_dataset.py rather than an argument about vibes.

nodes.label: House rule: the answer key is written by hand
nodes.norm_label: house rule: the answer key is written by hand
nodes.rationale: If a model writes the labels, scoring that model against them measures self-agreement and quietly penalises every other model for disagreeing. Every label is hand-written against a published rubric you can argue with.

nodes.label: Sequential runs preserve latency validity
nodes.rationale: Running the calls concurrently would finish sooner and make every latency number meaningless, because they would all be queued behind each other.

nodes.label: Deliberately awkward lead set
nodes.rationale: Roughly a third of the 60 leads are awkward on purpose: real buyers on personal email, competitors posing as buyers, huge companies with no fit, senior people with no intent, and two nearly empty messages. A test set of obvious cases puts every model at 100% and tells you nothing.

nodes.label: SYSTEM email-writing prompt
nodes.rationale: Conditions the email on the triage judgments already made, so an enterprise ready_to_buy lead gets a different email from a mid-market evaluating one. Bans generic openers, exclamation marks and em dashes; 10 of 29 outputs contained an em dash anyway.

nodes.label: CLI environment leak in generated emails
nodes.norm_label: cli environment leak in generated emails
nodes.rationale: 10 of 29 emails contain an em dash the prompt forbade, and the emails are signed with a name never supplied in the prompt, implying the CLI leaks something from the environment. Neither affects triage numbers since no judgment depends on a signature.

nodes.label: Step 6: write the first-touch email
nodes.rationale: 29 of 60 leads earned an email at a mean of 4,052 ms and $0.0026 each; the other 31 were rejected or nurtured and cost nothing to write to. The architecture is not 'Jev instead of Claude' but Jev deciding which leads are worth paying Claude for.

nodes.label: House rule: say where the other thing wins
nodes.norm_label: house rule: say where the other thing wins
nodes.rationale: Jev cannot write an email; rather than asserting that, the repo asks the live API for a text question type and shows the HTTP 400.

nodes.label: Jev has no text primitive (HTTP 400)
nodes.rationale: Jev exposes choice, score and noul and nothing that returns prose. Asking for text is not slow or bad, it is an api_usage_error. This is the step that makes the repo an architecture argument rather than a Jev advertisement.

nodes.label: Emails written only for ae_now and sdr_sequence leads
nodes.norm_label: emails written only for ae_now and sdr_sequence leads
nodes.rationale: Gating the expensive writing step on the cheap triage step is where the end-to-end saving comes from: 29 of 60 leads earned an email and the other 31 cost nothing to write to.

nodes.label: End-to-end cost per 1,000 inbound leads
nodes.rationale: Jev triage plus Sonnet writing costs $1.31 per 1,000 versus $4.28 for Sonnet doing both, 3.3x cheaper end to end, and the saving grows the worse your inbound is because junk never reaches the expensive step.

nodes.label: Split-call ablation (one Claude call per question)
nodes.norm_label: split-call ablation (one claude call per question)
nodes.rationale: Run to answer the 'you strawmanned Claude by asking four questions at once' objection. It helped: icp_fit 51.7% to 71.7%, route accuracy 53.3% to 61.7%, Brier nearly halved. It also cost 5.2x the latency and 2.9x the money and still lost to Jev by 28 points.

nodes.label: results.json (scored benchmark output)
nodes.rationale: Seven scored records: jev, claude-haiku-4-5 and claude-sonnet-5 at v1 and v2, plus the v1-split Haiku ablation. All seven report 60 completed leads and 0 failed calls.

nodes.label: Result record: claude-haiku-4-5
nodes.rationale: v1: 53.3% route accuracy, 2,630ms p50, $1.339 per 1,000, 7 of 16 funded buyers binned, Brier 0.365/0.383. Naming the competitors in v2 made it worse on routing (51.7%) and binned 9 of 16 buyers.

nodes.label: Result record: claude-haiku-4-5-split
nodes.rationale: The v1-split ablation: 61.7% route accuracy and icp_fit up to 71.7% with Brier nearly halved, at 13,631ms p50 and $3.933 per 1,000 across 4 calls per lead.

nodes.label: Result record: claude-sonnet-5
nodes.rationale: v1: 78.3% route accuracy, 2,571ms p50, $3.006 per 1,000, 1 of 16 buyers binned. v2 improves to 80.0% route accuracy, disqualify 90.0%, 0 buyers binned and 0 leaked, and cost falls to $2.22.

nodes.label: Sample-size caveat (60 leads, one laptop, one afternoon)
nodes.norm_label: sample-size caveat (60 leads, one laptop, one afternoon)
nodes.rationale: 60 cases carries roughly plus or minus 8 points at 90% confidence and latency depends on location relative to the API, so the reader should take the shape of the result rather than the third decimal place. Cost is the number to trust, being token counts against published rates.

nodes.label: Do not read the partial run
nodes.norm_label: do not read the partial run
nodes.rationale: At 18 leads the split run showed 88.9% route accuracy and looked like it had closed the gap; at 60 leads it was 61.7%.
